opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it was a bit of a culture shock at first. Coming from a background where the main goal was simply to get good grades and get into a good school, I assumed college would work the same way: study hard, do well on exams, and things would sort themselves out. But in the U.S., career development starts almost the moment you arrive on campus.

By freshman year, people around me were already talking about internships, networking events, and recruiting timelines. There were career fairs where students showed up in suits with stacks of résumés, and upperclassmen would tell you, "If you want a finance or consulting internship junior summer, you need to start preparing sophomore year." I remember feeling a little lost, because nobody had told me the game had started already.

What struck me most was how structured and almost industrialized it was. There were clubs dedicated to specific industries, investment clubs, consulting clubs, tech clubs, and they functioned almost like pipelines. Alumni would come back and coach you on case interviews or technical questions. Career services would review your résumé line by line. There was a very clear script for what a "successful" path looked like, and the most prestigious options were usually banking, consulting, or big tech.

On one hand, I really appreciated it. It taught me to be proactive, to reach out to people I didn't know, to articulate what I'd done and why it mattered. Those are skills I still use every day. On the other hand, I think it pushed a lot of us toward the same few paths without really asking whether that's what we wanted. Many people chose a job because it was the "default" good outcome, not because they had thought deeply about it.

For me, the most valuable part ended up being the exposure. Even if I didn't follow the standard script all the way, seeing how many different options existed, and realizing that you could design your own path rather than just follow one, really shaped how I thought about my career later on.

r001.rationale: The response says career preparation begins almost immediately and students discuss internships and recruiting in freshman year, but it does not say students are pressured to commit to a post-college career path then.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it took me a while to even understand that there was a "culture" around it. I came in freshman year thinking college was about taking classes and figuring out what I liked. Then, maybe three weeks into my first semester, I noticed people in my dorm already had their résumés formatted, they were going to recruiting events for finance and consulting, and they were talking about sophomore summer internships like it was urgent. I remember thinking, wait, we just got here, why are we already talking about leaving?

What struck me most was how early the pipeline starts and how structured it is. There are career-services offices, there are alumni networks, there are these clubs that are basically pre-professional training grounds. If you want to do investment banking, there's a club for it, and the upperclassmen will coach you on exactly what to say in interviews. Same for consulting, same for tech. It's very efficient, and I think for people who already know what they want, it's genuinely great.

But for me, coming from a different environment, it created a lot of anxiety. There's this feeling that if you're not on a track by sophomore year, you're behind. And the tracks that are most visible are the ones with the clearest recruiting timelines, so finance, consulting, software. If you're interested in something less legible, like research, or writing, or policy, you don't get that same scaffolding, and it can feel like the school is quietly telling you those paths matter less.

The other thing I'd say is the culture around talking about your career is very different from what I grew up with. Americans are comfortable self-promoting in a way that felt almost rude to me at first. You're expected to network, to reach out to strangers for coffee chats, to describe your own strengths confidently. I had to learn that. At first I felt like I was bragging every time I introduced myself. Later I realized it's just a different grammar for the same thing, and that not learning it would actually hurt me.

Looking back, I think the most valuable part wasn't the recruiting machinery itself. It was the peers. Being surrounded by people who were very intentional about their futures forced me to ask myself what I actually wanted, instead of just drifting. The culture was stressful, but it made me articulate things about myself that I otherwise would have avoided for years.

r001.rationale: The response describes students entering recruiting events within weeks of freshman year and says the early pipeline creates pressure to get on a career track by sophomore year.

astra-6.text: What stood out to me was how career development was treated as part of college life, something you could start exploring early. It wasn’t just, “Get your degree, and then figure out a job.” There was an emphasis on understanding your interests, talking to people, and trying different directions. I found that encouraging, although it could also create pressure to always have a plan. For me, the useful part was learning to see career choices as a process of exploration rather than one decision that determines everything.

r001.rationale: The response mentions exploring career options early and feeling pressure to always have a plan, but it does not say students were pressured to commit to a post-college career path in their first year.

I found that helpful, because it made the process feel more concrete, but it could also create pressure.
